strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of a new multi-modal variational bound, including a full 'ELBO surgery' style distribution-matching analysis (Proposition 1, Corollary 2) that clarifies exactly what the bound optimizes, in contrast to existing mixture-based bounds whose variational gap is provably non-vanishing (Daunhawer et al., 2022) even for infinite-capacity encoders.

Introduces a well-motivated generalization of PoE/MoE aggregation schemes via permutation-invariant (DeepSets, Set Transformer) architectures, with a careful theoretical justification via the Bloem-Reddy and Teh (2020) invariance characterization, and further extends this to permutation-equivariant schemes for models with private/shared latent variables.

Connects the framework to a broad set of related ideas (information bottleneck, rate-distortion/β-VAE analysis, meta-learning/Neural Processes, weak identifiability results building on Khemakhem et al./Lu et al.), giving the work strong theoretical breadth and originality in synthesizing these perspectives for the multi-modal setting.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple settings (linear Gaussian models with closed-form MLE comparison, non-linear identifiable models with known ground truth, and the MNIST-SVHN-Text benchmark), with consistent controlled comparisons (same hyperparameters across aggregation schemes and bounds) that isolate the effect of the bound vs. the aggregation scheme — a methodological strength lacking in much prior multi-modal VAE literature.
Thorough appendices with proofs, extra ablations (varying β, private latent variables, missingness), and detailed architecture/hyperparameter documentation supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper is very dense and long, with numerous remarks, examples, and side results (e.g., Remarks 3–25, multiple appendices) that could overwhelm readers and make it hard to discern the core message; some of this content (mixture models, missing modalities, time-series remark) feels tangential and underdeveloped relative to the main contribution.

The main practical bound requires sampling from two encoding distributions (qφ(z|xS) and qφ(z|x)) per gradient step, roughly doubling computational cost, and this trade-off versus mixture-based bounds is not quantified empirically (e.g., wall-clock time comparisons are absent).

Empirical results are somewhat mixed: Table 5/6/8 show the new bound is not uniformly better on generative coherence measures (e.g., less coherent for MNIST cross-generation, Table 6), and no single aggregation/bound configuration dominates across all metrics, which tempers the strength of the 'higher LLH' claim as a general practical recommendation.

The identifiability result (Proposition 15) is a fairly direct translation of Lu et al. (2022)'s unimodal result to the conditional multi-modal setting; while useful, the novelty of this specific theoretical contribution is incremental rather than fundamentally new, and the assumptions (strongly exponential family, injective decoders, Lebesgue densities) are restrictive and explicitly noted not to hold for manifold-supported data like images.

The MNIST-SVHN-Text experiments, while more controlled than prior work, still show that mixture-based bounds retain advantages for cross-reconstruction tasks, and the paper's own limitations section admits mixture bounds 'might be preferred' in cross-modal reconstruction-focused settings, suggesting the practical superiority of the proposed method is context-dependent rather than universal.

Some notational inconsistencies and typos are present (e.g., 'Lb\L' in the text after Corollary 2, inconsistent citation numbering 'Corollary 19' referring to what is labeled Corollary 2 in the main text), which could hinder careful reading and reproducibility of the proofs.

strengths: The paper provides a thorough and mathematically careful theoretical treatment: an ELBO-surgery-style analysis (Proposition 1, Corollary 2) connecting the proposed masked bound to distribution matching in both data and latent space, paralleling the well-known uni-modal VAE ELBO-surgery results.

The identification of a fundamental limitation of mixture-based multi-modal bounds (irreducible conditional-entropy gap, per Daunhawer et al. 2022) and the construction of a bound that can in principle become tight for infinite-capacity encoders is a clean and useful theoretical contribution.

The introduction of permutation-invariant/equivariant aggregation schemes (DeepSets- and Transformer-based) that generalize PoE/MoE/MoPoE is a natural and reasonably well-motivated extension, with care taken to preserve invariance/equivariance properties and to analyze interactions with private latent variables.

The weak identifiability result (Proposition 15), extending Lu et al. (2022) to the conditional multi-modal setting, is a nice connection between the proposed inference scheme and the identifiability literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning linear Gaussian models, non-linear identifiable (iVAE-style) models, and a tri-modal MNIST-SVHN-Text benchmark, with information-theoretic (rate-distortion) diagnostics that help interpret the behavior of different bounds/aggregation schemes rather than relying on a single scalar metric.
weaknesses: The claimed practical benefit of the new bound is inconsistent across the paper's own experiments: Tables 5, 6, 8-13 show that neither the new bound nor the PI aggregation schemes dominate across coherence, cross-generation, or latent-classification metrics; the mixture bound is often better for cross-modal coherence while the new bound is better for full reconstruction, so the headline claim of 'better' models is really a rate-distortion trade-off rather than a clear improvement, and this is only partially acknowledged in the conclusion.

The core theoretical contribution (bound combining a marginal ELBO on S with a conditional bound on the remainder, LS + L\S) is a fairly direct generalization of previously published two-term/triple-ELBO constructions (Wu & Goodman 2019 double VAE bound, Vedantam et al. 2018 triple-ELBO, Mita et al. 2021), which somewhat limits the originality of the central idea; the paper's own Example 6 acknowledges this lineage.

The presentation is extremely dense and encyclopedic (dozens of remarks, examples, and propositions in the main text, an enormous appendix), which harms readability and makes it difficult to identify the paper's single most important take-away; many remarks (e.g., Remarks 3-6, 9-14) read as a loosely connected list of observations rather than a focused argument, diluting the paper's impact despite genuine technical content.

The paper repeatedly acknowledges but does not quantify the added computational cost of the new bound (requires sampling from two encoders) or of the learnable PI aggregation schemes; no wall-clock or memory comparison is provided to help readers judge whether the reported LLH/coherence gains justify the overhead, despite this being listed as a 'limitation.'

The masking distribution ρ(S), which plays a central role in both bounds and is acknowledged to induce a Jensen gap and multi-task-learning-like gradient conflicts (Remark 6), is fixed to one particular hierarchical Bernoulli construction without ablation; sensitivity of results to this choice is not explored, despite it plausibly affecting which modalities are favored during training.

External baseline comparisons (MVAE, MMVAE, MoPoE, MMJSD, MVTCAE) are taken from the literature with different architectures/hyperparameters and are only loosely comparable to the paper's own controlled comparisons, which undercuts the paper's stated goal of 'a clearer disentanglement of how either the variational objective or the aggregation scheme affects different multi-modal evaluation measures.'

The private-latent-variable analysis in Section 3.2 shows that the straightforward SumPooling-based encoder does not, in general, respect the conditional independence structure implied by the generative model (information leakage from xS into private latents of unobserved modalities), and the proposed fix (permutation-equivariant construction) is not evaluated for whether it actually eliminates this leakage in practice, leaving a gap between theory and the empirical private-latent-variable experiments.

strengths: Provides a principled new variational bound for multi-modal VAEs that provably avoids the fundamental tightness limitation of mixture-based bounds identified by Daunhawer et al. (2022), with a clean ELBO-surgery style analysis (Proposition 1, Corollary 2) showing exactly what distributions are matched by each term of the bound.

Introduces a unifying, well-motivated family of permutation-invariant aggregation schemes (SumPooling/DeepSets and Set-Transformer/SelfAttention) that strictly generalize PoE, MoE, and MoPoE, backed by the Bloem-Reddy & Teh exchangeability theory, and extends these ideas naturally to permutation-equivariant encoders for models with private latent variables.

Provides a rigorous information-theoretic (rate-distortion) characterization of both the new bound and the mixture-based bound (Lemma 7, Corollary 8, Remark 9), clarifying the trade-offs (cross-rate regularization vs. cross-distortion optimization) in an interpretable way.

Extends weak identifiability results from the iVAE literature to the multi-modal conditional setting (Proposition 15), giving a theoretical grounding for why the proposed bound and flexible aggregation can help recover true latent structure.

Extensive and carefully controlled experiments (linear Gaussian models, non-linear identifiable models with auxiliary labels, and MNIST-SVHN-Text) that disentangle the effects of the variational bound choice and aggregation scheme, using matched hyperparameters/architectures across baselines - a methodological improvement over prior comparisons in this literature.
Thorough appendices with full proofs, additional ablations (different β, missing modalities, mixture priors), algorithmic pseudocode, and architecture details, supporting reproducibility.

Thoughtful discussion of limitations (added compute cost, scalability of self-attention) and of connections to a wide swath of related work (CCA, neural processes, contrastive learning, diffusion priors), situating the contribution well within the literature.
weaknesses: The paper is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many remarks, examples, and cross-referenced propositions), which may hinder accessibility and risks obscuring the core practical takeaways for readers less steeped in this specific sub-literature.

No single bound/aggregation combination dominates across all empirical metrics; e.g., in MNIST-SVHN-Text experiments the mixture-based bound is often more coherent for cross-generating certain modalities and yields better unsupervised latent classification accuracy (Table 13), partially undercutting the headline claim of straightforward superiority.

The added computational cost of the method (requiring two encoder samples per step, plus trainable aggregation functions) is acknowledged but not empirically quantified (e.g., wall-clock or memory overhead), leaving practitioners without clear guidance on the cost-benefit trade-off.

The identifiability result (Proposition 15) is largely a direct translation/application of an existing theorem (Lu et al., 2022) to the multi-modal conditional setting rather than a fundamentally new theoretical development.

Real-data experiments are limited to a single moderate-scale benchmark (MNIST-SVHN-Text); there is no evaluation on larger-scale or more heterogeneous real-world multi-modal datasets (e.g., multi-omics or vision-language data mentioned in the introduction as motivation), leaving the practical significance at scale less established.

Self-attention-based aggregation scales quadratically in the number of modalities, which may limit applicability to settings with many modalities, and this scalability concern is only briefly noted rather than empirically explored.
